passage:
At the dinner table in their Odisha town house, Yash's father set down his spoon. "The papers say these machines will take every job. And your brain will go soft."
Yash's mother nodded. Yash's ears grew hot, but he didn't argue.
The next evening he pulled a chair beside them and opened his laptop. "Here is what I actually do with it." He showed them the maths steps it had explained and the essay questions he had written himself. Aadhya, his younger sister, added, "He never lets me use it for homework."
They agreed on one hour a day, with the screen open in the hall. Then his father asked, "And what will still matter when you're grown?" "Asking good questions," Yash said. "And being kind to customers." His father laughed.

qa.q: How long a limit did the family agree on?
qa.a: They agreed on one hour a day.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling when his father spoke, and why did he not argue?
qa.a: His ears grew hot, which suggests hurt or defensiveness, but he chose to show his parents what he really uses it for rather than argue at the table.

qa.q: What made Yash's approach work with his parents?
qa.a: He listened first, showed real examples, agreed on limits and talked about skills that stay valuable. 😊

qa.q: What might Yash's father be worried about?
qa.a: He fears for his son's future and mind because the papers say machines will take jobs, so seeing real use and limits eases that worry.

grounding: Shows a teen answering parents' fears about AI by showing his use, agreeing limits and naming lasting skills.

passage:
In Malegaon, Rafiq's Abbu ran a small tailoring shop, and he did not trust machines he couldn't open with a screwdriver.

"This AI business," he said on Sunday, watching Rafiq on the phone. "It will eat your brain. And your job. Your cousin in Mumbai lost his data entry job to a computer."

Rafiq felt irritated, then saw his father's hands, tight on the cloth. He was afraid.

"Abbu, come see what I actually do." He showed him: asking the chatbot to explain English grammar, then practising his own sentences. Checking his answers to maths problems he had already solved.

His elder sister Reena, sewing buttons in the corner, added, "It's like a tutor that's awake at night, Abbu. But he still has to do the work."

Abbu frowned at the screen for a long time. "One hour a day," he said. "And no homework answers from it."

"Deal. And Abbu, it can't do what you do. It can't measure a person and make a sherwani that fits." Abbu almost smiled.

qa.q: What kind of shop did Rafiq's Abbu run?
qa.a: Abbu ran a small tailoring shop.

qa.q: What was Abbu feeling as he spoke about the AI?
qa.a: Abbu was afraid, with his hands tight on the cloth, worried AI would harm Rafiq's mind and future.

qa.q: How did Rafiq respond to Abbu's worry in a wise way?
qa.a: Rafiq showed Abbu exactly how he used the chatbot, agreed to a one-hour limit and no homework answers, and pointed out skills AI cannot replace.

qa.q: How does Reena see the AI?
qa.a: Reena sees it as a night-time tutor that helps, but only if Rafiq still does the work himself.

grounding: It shows a teen whose parent fears AI will ruin his future, showing what he uses it for, agreeing on limits and talking about skills that stay valuable.
